title: Shwedagon
hookLine: the golden stupa of Yangon, said to hold hairs of the Buddha

lines: A GOLDEN BELL AGAINST THE SKY.
cards: Shoes off at the bottom of the stairs. Everyone climbs barefoot.

At the top, a wide platform opens out around a great golden stupa, shaped like a bell, narrowing to a spire, blazing in the afternoon sun and ringed by smaller shrines. People walk around it slowly, clockwise.
Some sit to meditate. Some chant. Some pour water over a small Buddha image at a corner shrine.
This is the Shwedagon, in Yangon.

teach.b: First, the story. The Vinaya tells of two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, who meet the Buddha soon after his awakening, offer him food, and become his first lay followers.

Later tradition adds what the Vinaya doesn't say: the Buddha gave them hairs from his head. Burmese tradition says they carried them home, where the hairs were enshrined on a hill. That hill is where the Shwedagon stands.
The stupa is covered in gold, given over generations by rulers and ordinary people; tradition at the site remembers a queen who gave her own weight in gold.
Visitors still press small squares of gold leaf onto Buddha images. The shine is made of gifts. Third, the corners.
Around the base are shrines for the days of the week, by the Burmese way of counting them.

teach.h: A SHRINE FOR YOUR BIRTH DAY.
teach.b: People go to the shrine for the day they were born, pour water over the Buddha image there, and make offerings, so each person on the platform brings something of their own: their birthday, their family's wishes, their troubles.

teach.h: WALK AROUND, KEEP IT ON THE RIGHT.
teach.b: Like the stupas of Sanchi, it is a reliquary, a mound built around something precious, and walking around it clockwise, keeping it on the right, is a way of honoring what is inside.
Nobody sees the hairs. As at Kandy, people honor what they cannot see, and what they bring is gold, water, flowers, and the simple act of walking around.

how: Visitors to the Shwedagon climb barefoot, walk clockwise around the stupa, offer flowers, candles and gold leaf, and pour water over the Buddha image at the shrine for the day of the week they were born.

o: a royal palace roofed in gold in Mandalay
a hilltop monastery where young monks study
the golden stupa of Yangon, circled barefoot

p: pressed onto images as a gift
keeping the stupa on your right

s: the Vinaya itself says the hairs were enshrined in Yangon
the Vinaya tells of the meal and the merchants following the Buddha; the hairs come from later tradition, and their journey to Yangon from Burmese tradition.
pilgrims walk around the Shwedagon clockwise
keeping the stupa on the right is a way of honoring what is inside.
people go to the corner shrine for the day they were born
they pour water over the Buddha image there and make offerings.

games.q: you're one of the two merchants. the Buddha has given you hairs from his head. what do you do?
o: keep them in your purse as a souvenir.
carry them home and enshrine them.
give them to the first king you meet.
games.why: Burmese tradition says the merchants carried the hairs home, where they were enshrined on the hill where the Shwedagon now stands.

practice: Picture warm stone under bare feet and a golden stupa ahead, wide at the base and narrowing to a point against the sky, and walk around it slowly in your mind, clockwise, one step for each breath.
At the center, let there be whatever you most want to honor; if you pray, you can bring a line you already know.

wordCard.voice: Shwedagon. The golden stupa of Yangon, said by Burmese tradition to hold hairs of the Buddha, circled by barefoot pilgrims. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: cetiya, a shrine or stupa, a place of honor like the Shwedagon.

carryVoice: Your line: the golden stupa. Barefoot, clockwise, and nobody in a hurry. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Burmese tradition of the Shwedagon (the hair relics enshrined on Singuttara hill)
